ancient-necromancy.alt: A Greek black-figure vase painting of the underworld, with a bearded figure bent forward pushing a large white boulder.
ancient-necromancy.caption: The underworld on an Attic vase. Every ancient account of consulting the dead is working from a picture like this one.

greek-magical-gems.alt: A carved oval gemstone showing a figure with a rooster's head, holding a shield and whip, with serpents in place of legs.
greek-magical-gems.caption: A magical gem cut with Abraxas. Not one of the medical types — but the same craft, the same workshops, and the same unpronounceable words.

mithraism-seven-grades.alt: A black-and-white Roman mosaic panel showing a raven, a small drinking cup and a herald's staff, set in a plain border.
mithraism-seven-grades.caption: The first rung: Corax, the Raven. A bird, a cup, and Mercury's staff, laid into the floor at Ostia.

ancient-binding-spells-law.alt: A thin rectangular sheet of grey lead covered in small scratched Greek letters.
ancient-binding-spells-law.caption: A lead binding tablet from Pella, fourth century BCE. Not a judicial curse itself, but the same cheap technology every courtroom curse used.

evil-eye-ancient-world.alt: A bronze wind chime from Pompeii in the form of a winged phallus, with small bells suspended beneath it on chains.
evil-eye-ancient-world.caption: A tintinnabulum from Pompeii. Hung in a doorway or garden, it caught the light, made noise, and was meant to be funny.

ancient-mystery-cults-guide.alt: Marble relief showing Demeter handing grain to the boy Triptolemos, with Persephone standing behind him holding a torch.
ancient-mystery-cults-guide.caption: The Great Eleusinian Relief: Demeter, Triptolemos and Persephone. Around 440–430 BCE.

eleusinian-mysteries-telesterion.alt: The excavated foundations of the Telesterion at Eleusis, a large square hall cut into a rocky hillside.
eleusinian-mysteries-telesterion.caption: What remains of the Telesterion — the hall that held several thousand initiates at once.

eleusinian-kykeon-psychedelic.alt: A votive marble relief from Eleusis depicting Demeter, Persephone and Triptolemos with sheaves of grain.
eleusinian-kykeon-psychedelic.caption: Grain, and the goddesses who controlled it. Votive relief from Eleusis, fourth century BCE.

orphic-gold-tablets.alt: A small rectangular sheet of gold leaf covered in tiny incised Greek letters, displayed in a museum case.
orphic-gold-tablets.caption: The Petelia tablet. Instructions for the dead, small enough to fold into a palm.

mithras-tauroctony-decoded.alt: A carved marble relief of Mithras in a Phrygian cap kneeling on a bull and stabbing its neck, with a dog, snake and scorpion.
mithras-tauroctony-decoded.caption: The tauroctony. The same scene appears in almost every mithraeum ever excavated.

villa-of-the-mysteries-frescoes.alt: A wide section of Roman wall painting on a deep red ground, showing near-life-size robed figures standing in a row.
villa-of-the-mysteries-frescoes.caption: Part of the frieze in Room 5. Twenty-nine figures, and no agreement about what they are doing.

greek-magical-papyri.alt: A fragment of ancient papyrus densely written in Greek and Demotic script, with some lines picked out in red ink.
greek-magical-papyri.caption: A working spellbook from Roman Egypt. The instructions are in black; the formulae in red.

ancient-curse-tablets.alt: A small irregular sheet of grey lead covered in scratched Latin lettering.
ancient-curse-tablets.caption: A lead curse tablet from Bath, complaining about a theft. Scratched, folded, and thrown into the spring.

sibylline-books-rome.alt: A long trapezoidal rock-cut corridor at Cumae, lit by openings along one side, receding into darkness.
sibylline-books-rome.caption: The corridor at Cumae, long identified with the Sibyl's cave.

damnatio-memoriae.alt: A circular painted panel showing the Roman imperial family, with the face of one of the two sons deliberately scraped away.
damnatio-memoriae.caption: The Severan Tondo. Geta's face was removed by hand, on his brother's orders.

library-of-alexandria-what-was-lost.alt: Ruined stone foundations and a tall standing column at the Serapeum site in Alexandria.
library-of-alexandria-what-was-lost.caption: The Serapeum of Alexandria. What is left of the daughter library.
library-of-alexandria-what-was-lost.credit: Institute for the Study of the Ancient World

oracle-of-the-dead-ephyra.alt: Thick polygonal stone walls of a ruined Hellenistic building standing on a low hill.
oracle-of-the-dead-ephyra.caption: The building at Mesopotamos. Thick walls, a big cellar, and a granary.

piacenza-liver-etruscan.alt: A bronze model of a sheep's liver, its flat surface divided into many small compartments each carrying an inscription.
piacenza-liver-etruscan.caption: The Piacenza Liver. Forty compartments, forty gods, and a map of the sky.

samothrace-great-gods.alt: A headless, armless marble statue of a winged woman in wind-blown drapery, standing on the prow of a ship.
samothrace-great-gods.caption: The Nike of Samothrace, unearthed in the Sanctuary of the Great Gods in 1863.

bacchanalia-186-bce.alt: A rectangular bronze tablet densely inscribed with Latin text, its surface worn and pitted with age.
bacchanalia-186-bce.caption: The Senatus consultum de Bacchanalibus. Found at Tiriolo in 1640, still readable.

cult-of-isis-rome.alt: A marble statue of the goddess Isis draped in a fringed mantle, holding a sistrum, with a solar disc and serpent on her head.
cult-of-isis-rome.caption: Isis, sculpted in Rome under Hadrian. She holds her sistrum; Egypt had left the statue in every way but the stone.

books-augustus-burned.alt: A marble statue of a man in a heavy toga with a fold of the cloth drawn up over his head, both forearms broken away, standing against a dark red wall.
books-augustus-burned.caption: Augustus with his head veiled for sacrifice, in the dress of the priesthood he had waited twenty-three years to hold.

liber-linteus.alt: Long horizontal strips of ancient linen, stained deep red-brown, each carrying rows of small dark Etruscan letters, mounted against a black backing.
liber-linteus.caption: The Liber Linteus, reassembled. Every strip here was once wound around a body.

etruscan-language-lost.alt: Three thin rectangular sheets of gold displayed side by side, each crumpled slightly and covered in rows of incised ancient lettering, with small nail holes around their edges.
etruscan-language-lost.caption: The Pyrgi Tablets: two in Etruscan, one in Phoenician. The nearest thing to a bilingual, and not near enough.

claudius-etruscan-history.alt: A large bronze plaque engraved with two dense columns of Latin capitals, split by a ragged vertical break down the centre and broken away along the top edge.
claudius-etruscan-history.caption: The Lyon Tablet. Low in the left-hand column Claudius tells the Senate that the Etruscans called the king Rome knew as Servius Tullius by another name: Mastarna.

delphi-pythia.alt: The interior of a Greek red-figure cup: a woman sits on a tall tripod, head bowed over a shallow bowl held in one hand and a laurel sprig in the other, facing a bearded man in a wreath who stands wrapped in his cloak.
delphi-pythia.caption: A consultation, painted around 440 BCE. The seated figure is usually identified as Themis rather than the Pythia — it is still the closest thing we have to a contemporary picture of the procedure.

delphi-gases-hypothesis.alt: Looking down into the excavated stone foundations of the temple of Apollo at Delphi: courses of large limestone blocks around a sunken rectangular space, with a wooded hillside beyond.
delphi-gases-hypothesis.caption: Under the floor of the temple. This is where the excavators went looking for a chasm, and did not find one.

dream-incubation-asclepius.alt: A marble votive relief: a bearded god treats the bare shoulder of a standing young man, while to the right the same young man lies asleep on a couch with a large snake stretched over his shoulder.
dream-incubation-asclepius.caption: Incubation in one panel: the treatment, and the dream. Dedicated by a man named Archinos — his name is cut along the base — at the sanctuary of Amphiaraos at Oropos, not Epidaurus. A different healer, the same procedure.

etruscan-lightning-doctrine.alt: A slender nude bronze statuette of a standing male figure, one arm extended holding a forked thunderbolt, the other raised holding a small round object.
etruscan-lightning-doctrine.caption: Tinia, the Etruscan sky god, with the weapon in his hand. Eight other gods were entitled to throw one, and his worst needed permission.

numas-buried-books.alt: Both faces of a Roman silver denarius: on the left a bearded head in profile wearing a diadem inscribed NVMA, on the right the prow of a galley with lettering above and below.
numas-buried-books.caption: Numa on a denarius struck for Pompey in 49 BCE, his name cut into the diadem. Seven centuries after his supposed reign, a Roman family was still advertising him as an ancestor.

roman-augury-sacred-chickens.alt: The reverse of a Roman silver denarius of Vespasian, showing a set of priestly religious implements including an augur's curved lituus staff.
roman-augury-sacred-chickens.caption: A lituus on a denarius of Vespasian. The augur's badge of office, not a chicken in sight, and still the symbol the whole discipline ran on.
roman-augury-sacred-chickens.credit: West Yorkshire Archaeology Service, Anna Marshall, 2004-05-17 11:35:27

cult-of-cybele-taurobolium.alt: A carved marble altar from the fourth century CE showing Cybele enthroned with her hand on the shoulder of Attis, flanked by pine trees.
cult-of-cybele-taurobolium.caption: A taurobolium altar dedicated around 360 CE, showing Cybele and Attis. Set up by a man who had just undergone the very rite Prudentius later wrote up as savage.

andania-mysteries-inscription.alt: A wide green valley in Messenia seen from a hillside, with the excavated ruins of ancient Messene laid out among olive groves and mountains beyond.
andania-mysteries-inscription.caption: The Messenian countryside, with ancient Messene in the middle distance. The festival regulated by the stone was held at Andania, elsewhere in this region.

cabeirion-thebes.alt: Detail of a Greek black-figure vase: a seated figure with an exaggerated grotesque face and a patterned headband holds out a small jug and a leafy sprig towards a standing figure with wild spiky hair.
cabeirion-thebes.caption: Herakles and Omphale, painted for the sanctuary outside Thebes. The style is the point. These are the heroes of Greek myth, drawn deliberately badly.

sack-of-eleusis-396.alt: Large fallen marble blocks, their faces carved with rows of projecting knobs, lying on stone paving at Eleusis with a rock-cut terrace rising behind them.
sack-of-eleusis-396.caption: Fallen blocks at Eleusis. The sanctuary initiated people for roughly two thousand years, and not one of them wrote down what happened in the hall.
